data.heading: Visiting a mosque: a guide for neighbors
data.body:
If you've never been inside a mosque, you're very welcome to visit [Islamic Center Name]. Here's what to expect.

It's best to contact us first. We can arrange a time that doesn't clash with prayers and ask someone to show you around and answer questions.

When you arrive, you'll be asked to remove your shoes before entering the prayer hall. There are shelves near the entrance. [Describe your dress guidance for visitors here.]

If you visit at prayer time, you're welcome to sit quietly at the back and watch. The prayer includes standing, bowing and prostrating together in rows, and it lasts a few minutes.

Please ask before taking photos, and avoid walking directly in front of someone who is praying.

After your visit, there's usually time for tea and questions. No question is too simple. Many visitors ask about the prayers, the building and daily life in our community.

We also hold open days during the year, which are a relaxed way to visit with others. Check our events page or send us a message to arrange a visit.

data.heading: Ramadan at the center
data.body:
Ramadan is the month in which Muslims fast from dawn until sunset. It's a special time at [Islamic Center Name], and the center is busier than at any other time of year.

Each evening, the fast is broken at Maghrib with iftar. We hold community iftars on [days], and everyone is welcome. [Add whether people should book.]

After Isha, we hold taraweeh prayers. [Add the time, and any details about the sisters' area or children.]

Because the start of Ramadan and Eid depends on the moon, exact dates are confirmed close to the time. We share them by [email / social media / this website].

If you'd like to help, we always need volunteers to set up, serve food and clean up after iftar. It's a wonderful way to meet people.

Neighbors who aren't Muslim are very welcome to join an iftar and learn more. Just let us know you're coming.
